lessons.title: China in 1945: A Country at the Crossroads
lessons.description: How war, warlordism and two rival armies set the stage for civil war in 1945.
lessons.content_html:
A Country in Ruins

When Japan surrendered in August 1945, China was not at peace. Eight years of Japanese invasion had killed an estimated 14–20 million Chinese people, displaced tens of millions more and gutted the cities the Guomindang government depended on. Inflation was rampant, the railways were broken and a generation of young men had been conscripted, killed or scattered. Behind that ruin stood a longer crisis: since the fall of the Qing dynasty in 1911, China had been fractured by warlord armies, foreign concessions and a republican government that never fully controlled its own territory.

Key Fact

By 1945 China had endured 34 years of upheaval — warlord rule from 1916 and full Japanese invasion from 1937. The country that emerged from the Sino-Japanese War was exhausted, divided and ready for civil war.

The Guomindang in 1945: Strong on Paper, Weak in Reality

Chiang Kai-shek led the Guomindang (GMD) and the Republic of China government from his wartime capital of Chongqing. On the surface, the GMD looked unbeatable. It commanded a regular army of around 4.3 million soldiers, controlled the major cities, held a seat on the new United Nations Security Council, and received steady American aid — eventually about $3 billion between 1945 and 1949. American transport planes and ships moved GMD troops into former Japanese-held territory faster than the communists could reach it.

Beneath this surface, however, the GMD was hollow. Wartime hyperinflation was wiping out salaries and savings — by 1948 it took a wheelbarrow of banknotes to buy a sack of rice. Officials were widely seen as corrupt, hoarding US aid for personal enrichment. Conscription was brutal: peasant villages were ordered to supply soldiers, and recruits were often roped together to stop them deserting. The Guomindang relied on the cities, but the cities were where inflation hurt most.

It is tempting to treat August 1945 as a clean reset — Japan goes home, the civil war begins. The reality is messier. Japanese troops in northern China were ordered by the Allies to surrender to the GMD, but Soviet forces in Manchuria handed captured Japanese weapons to the CCP’s Eighth Route Army instead. Refugees, conscript soldiers and stranded Japanese civilians clogged the roads. Most of the country that the GMD now claimed to rule had been governed by puppet regimes, warlords or communist guerrillas for years. The civil war did not start on a blank slate.

The CCP in 1945: Yan’an, Land Reform and the Long March Story

Mao Zedong led the Chinese Communist Party from the dusty cave town of Yan’an in the north-west, where the party had retreated after the Long March of 1934–35. The CCP’s army — the Eighth Route Army and the New Fourth Army, later renamed the People’s Liberation Army — numbered roughly one million troops. On every measurable count of equipment and air power, the GMD was stronger. But the CCP had built two assets the GMD could not match.

First, the CCP had used the Sino-Japanese War to build a peasant base. In areas it controlled, the party reduced rents, redistributed land from absentee landlords and ran literacy classes. Soldiers in the Red Army were under orders not to steal from villages or harm civilians — a code known as the ‘Three Rules of Discipline and Eight Points of Attention’. The contrast with looting GMD conscripts was stark, and recruiters for the communists turned the difference into propaganda. Second, Mao had used Yan’an to consolidate his own leadership. The Rectification Campaign of 1942–44 purged rivals such as Wang Ming, while the legend of the Long March was carefully shaped after the fact to present Mao as the indispensable leader.

The Long March is the founding myth of the CCP — a year-long retreat over 5,600 miles, crossing rivers and snow-capped passes. The numbers are humbling: around 86,000 set out from Jiangxi in October 1934 and roughly 8,000 reached Yan’an in October 1935. But the historian Sun Shuyun and the Historical Association both stress that the heroic narrative was built afterwards. During the March itself Mao manoeuvred against rival communist leaders, especially Zhang Guotao, and the propaganda value of the March only grew with retelling. Strong answers acknowledge the March mattered for survival and for Mao’s personal authority — but treat the ‘heroic origin’ story as constructed, not given.

The Marshall Mediation, 1945–46

In August 1945 Mao flew to Chongqing to negotiate with Chiang Kai-shek under American pressure. The talks produced a fragile truce. President Truman then sent General George C. Marshall to broker a coalition government and a unified army. For most of 1946, Marshall shuttled between the two sides. Zhou Enlai, Mao’s chief negotiator, played for time. Chiang doubted Marshall’s promises of further aid and used the lull to position GMD divisions in Manchuria. Local fighting never really stopped, and by January 1947 Marshall returned to Washington and declared his mission a failure. The full-scale civil war that followed was therefore not a sudden outbreak but a return to the path that Japan’s surrender had only briefly interrupted.

Key Fact

The GMD entered 1945 with 4.3 million soldiers, the cities, the UN seat and US aid — but with hyperinflation, corruption, brutal conscription and a hollowed-out countryside. The CCP had a smaller army of around 1 million but a tested rural base, disciplined troops and a unified leadership under Mao at Yan’an.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For Paper 3 inference questions on this period, focus on what a source implies about CCP or GMD strength — not just what it states. Quote one short detail and draw one inference from it; a paragraph of paraphrase will score lower than a tight, supported point. For interpretation questions later in the unit, examiners reward students who can name competing schools of thought (the heroic CCP narrative versus revisionist Western historians like Frank Dikötter and Sun Shuyun) rather than just describing what one historian says.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • By 1945 China had been at war or fragmented for over three decades — the civil war began on a country, and a peasantry, that were already exhausted.
  • The Guomindang held the cities, the army on paper and US backing, but was hollowed out by hyperinflation, corruption and an unpopular conscription system.
  • The CCP at Yan’an had built a disciplined peasant army, a record of land reform in liberated zones and a unified leadership under Mao — the Marshall mediation only briefly delayed open war.

practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Make an Inference from a Source
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two distinct, accurately phrased inferences. Each is anchored to a specific quoted detail from the source (for example, the GMD’s 4.3-million-strong regular army or US transport planes ferrying troops). Inferences go beyond surface description — e.g. that the GMD looked dominant on paper, but its strength was concentrated in cities. [4]

Developing: One supported inference plus a second point that is closer to a paraphrase of the source than an inference. [2]

practice_questions.text:
Study Interpretations 1 and 2. They give different views about the position of the Chinese Communist Party in 1945.
What is the main difference between these views? Explain your answer using details from both interpretations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A precise statement of the central difference (e.g. one interpretation presents the CCP as battle-hardened and well-prepared by Yan’an reforms; the other stresses how small and exposed the party was compared with the GMD). Each side of the difference is supported with a quoted or closely paraphrased detail from the matching interpretation. [4]

practice_questions.text:
Suggest one reason why Interpretations 1 and 2 may give different views about the strengths of the CCP in 1945.
You may use the sources from the section before to help explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: One clearly explained reason — e.g. the historians wrote at different times (Cold War-era versus post-archival access from the 1990s); they used different evidence (CCP-published material versus revisionist Western archival research, e.g. Frank Dikötter); or they had different purposes (commemorative versus critical). The reason is supported by a specific detail from the relevant interpretation or its provenance. [4]
Secure: A relevant reason explained, supported by detail but more thinly. [3]
Developing: A reason identified (e.g. ‘the historians have different opinions’) but with limited explanation of how that produces the difference. [2]
Emerging: Restates that the interpretations differ without explaining why; or names a reason without supporting it. [1]

practice_questions.text:
How far do you agree with Interpretation 2 about the relative strengths of the CCP and the Guomindang in 1945?
Explain your answer, using both interpretations and your knowledge of the historical context.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Examines BOTH interpretations as views (not as evidence), cross-referencing arguments and details. Uses own contextual knowledge of 1945 China — GMD army size, hyperinflation, corruption, US aid; CCP land reform, Yan’an base, Long March mythology — to weigh each view. Reaches a substantiated judgement that explicitly answers ‘how far’ rather than ‘which is right’. [13–16]
Secure: Both interpretations are reviewed and supported with own knowledge, but the cross-referencing is uneven, or the judgement is stated rather than fully argued. [9–12]
Developing: One interpretation is examined more than the other; own knowledge is used but in patches. The judgement is implicit. [5–8]
Emerging: Drifts into a general essay on 1945 China and barely engages with the interpretations as views; or relies on the stimulus alone. [1–4]

lessons.title: Civil War and Communist Victory, 1945-49
lessons.description: Why a peasant guerrilla army defeated a US-backed government and proclaimed the PRC.
lessons.content_html:
A War of Two Halves

The Chinese Civil War of 1946–49 falls neatly into two phases. In the opening eighteen months, the Guomindang (GMD) seemed to be winning. Chiang Kai-shek’s armies pushed into communist territory, captured the CCP capital of Yan’an in March 1947 and dominated almost every major city. By the autumn of 1948, however, the picture had reversed. In just over a year, the People’s Liberation Army (PLA) destroyed the GMD field armies in three campaigns, marched into Beijing without a fight and forced Chiang to flee for Taiwan. To explain Mao’s victory, examiners want to see leadership, military choices and the collapse of GMD legitimacy in the cities all weighed against each other — not military genius alone.

Key Fact

Three decisive 1948–49 campaigns ended the war: Liaoshen (Sept–Nov 1948, Manchuria), Huaihai (Nov 1948–Jan 1949, central China) and Pingjin (Nov 1948–Jan 1949, Beijing–Tianjin). Together they cost the GMD about 1.5 million troops.

CCP Strategy in the Countryside

From 1946, the CCP traded cities for countryside. Mao called it ‘luring the enemy in deep’. When GMD divisions advanced into communist zones, PLA units melted away, broke into smaller groups and harassed supply lines. The GMD seized empty towns; the PLA kept its soldiers and its peasant base. While Chiang’s armies thinned themselves out garrisoning captured cities, Lin Biao quietly built a powerful conventional force in Manchuria, supplied with captured Japanese weapons that the Soviets had passed to the CCP in 1945–46.

Behind the lines the party stepped up land reform. The Outline Land Law of October 1947 declared that all land would be redistributed equally; landlords were denounced in mass meetings and tens of thousands were killed. The reform was violent and not always popular — some ‘middle peasants’ lost out — but it bound the rural population to the CCP. Peasants who received land had a direct stake in the communist victory and were a steady source of recruits.

Examiners reward students who treat the CCP victory as multi-causal. Mao’s flexible strategy and the discipline of Lin Biao’s armies clearly mattered, but so did GMD self-destruction. Hyperinflation, corruption, brutal conscription and student protest in the cities meant Chiang lost the war in two places at once — on the battlefield and in the urban classroom and marketplace. Strong answers weigh CCP strengths against GMD failings rather than choosing one side of the equation.

The Guomindang Collapse in the Cities

While Mao consolidated the countryside, Chiang’s urban support disintegrated. By August 1948 the Chinese yuan had become worthless: a single US dollar bought 12 million yuan. The GMD launched the ‘gold yuan’ currency reform that month, ordering citizens to exchange gold and silver for new notes — the new notes also collapsed within weeks. Civil servants could no longer afford rice. University students protested against corruption and conscription, and were beaten by GMD police. American visitors who had been sympathetic to Chiang — including journalists and US Marshall Mission staff — began describing his regime as terminal.

The American government noticed. From mid-1948 the United States began winding down direct aid: the ‘China White Paper’ published by the State Department in August 1949 effectively wrote off the GMD. Madame Chiang Kai-shek (Soong Mei-ling) toured Washington begging for emergency funds, and was politely refused. The lesson examiners want students to draw is that c.$3 billion in US aid had not bought political legitimacy — the problem was internal.

The Decisive Year, 1948

From September 1948, Lin Biao opened the Liaoshen Campaign. Within seven weeks, around 470,000 GMD troops were killed or captured and Manchuria fell. The PLA inherited Japanese-built arsenals, railways and 600,000 captured rifles. Three weeks later, the Huaihai Campaign opened in central China. Over two months, around 555,000 GMD soldiers were destroyed across a battlefield north of the Yangtze. By January 1949 the Pingjin Campaign closed the trap on Beijing — the GMD garrison surrendered without a fight, and the PLA marched into the old imperial capital on 31 January.

Urban unrest is on the spec for a reason. By 1947–48 the cities the GMD relied on were in chaos: shopkeepers shut their doors against worthless currency, students staged hunger strikes against corruption (the ‘Anti-Hunger, Anti-Civil-War’ movement of 1947), and civil servants drifted away from work because their salaries had no purchasing power. The CCP had communist activists in many universities, and underground urban networks ran propaganda and intelligence. Examiners reward students who can connect the rural war to the urban collapse — one without the other does not explain 1949.

1 October 1949: The People’s Republic

On 1 October 1949, Mao stood on the Tiananmen rostrum and proclaimed the People’s Republic of China. The image — broadcast and printed in posters within hours — became one of the iconic moments of the twentieth century. By December, Chiang Kai-shek had retreated with his remaining troops, the GMD government and a substantial portion of China’s gold reserves to the island of Taiwan, where the Republic of China would survive as a separate state. Mao now ruled around 540 million people. The CCP had grown from c.40,000 members in 1937 to roughly 4.5 million in 1949.

Key Fact

By October 1949 Mao’s victory had several roots: PLA strategy and discipline (military), GMD corruption and brutal conscription (political), and hyperinflation that destroyed urban GMD legitimacy (economic). Each fed the other; no single factor is enough on its own.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When you face a 12-mark causation question on this topic, never reduce the CCP victory to one factor. Examiner reports for Paper 3 modern depth options reward answers that weigh several causes — CCP leadership, GMD failings, the role of land reform, urban collapse — against each other and reach a substantiated judgement. Use the stimulus points as scaffolding but always add a third cause from your own knowledge: relying only on the prompt is explicitly penalised.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • In phase one (1946–47) the GMD held cities; in phase two (1948–49) the PLA destroyed Chiang’s field armies in the Liaoshen, Huaihai and Pingjin campaigns.
  • CCP land reform and the discipline of the Red Army won rural support; GMD hyperinflation, corruption and conscription lost urban support.
  • Mao proclaimed the People’s Republic on 1 October 1949 and Chiang Kai-shek retreated to Taiwan in December — the CCP victory was multi-causal, not the product of military genius alone.

lessons.title: Establishing Communist Rule and the Korean War, 1949-53
lessons.description: How Mao consolidated the new state, allied with Stalin, and intervened in the Korean War.
lessons.content_html:
From Civil War to Government

Winning a civil war is not the same as ruling a country. By October 1949, the CCP had to govern around 540 million people across territory the size of a continent — collecting taxes, running schools and hospitals, and replacing GMD officials with party-trained cadres. Mao’s answer was to fuse the party, the new state and the army into one machine, with himself at its head. This lesson looks at three things: what Mao’s ideology actually said, how the new state was organised, and how the Korean War tested both at once.

Key Fact

Mao’s ideology blended Marxism-Leninism, the ‘mass line’ (party policy shaped by listening to peasants) and democratic centralism (debate within the party, total obedience once a decision is made). After 1949, this was filtered through the ‘cult of Mao’ — a personality cult that made him the symbol of the entire revolution.

Mao’s Ideology and Authority

Marxism-Leninism — the doctrine Mao inherited from Lenin’s Russia — argued that the urban industrial working class would lead the revolution. Mao’s twist was to make the peasantry the engine instead, fitting Chinese conditions where over 80 per cent of the population worked the land. He summed this up as the ‘mass line’: the party listens to the masses, takes their scattered ideas, sharpens them into policy, and returns them as orders. In practice the listening was selective; the orders were not. The other half of Mao’s framework was democratic centralism: debate inside the party, total obedience once a decision was reached.

Mao’s personal dominance was not automatic. He had defeated rivals like Wang Ming and Zhang Guotao at Yan’an, and after 1949 he still had to manage senior comrades — Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai, Lin Biao, Deng Xiaoping — who held substantial authority of their own. What set Mao apart was his record. He was credited with the survival of the Long March, the Yan’an base, and the victory of 1949. From 1950 onwards, propaganda departments ramped up the cult of Mao through portraits, songs, posters and Liu Shaoqi’s influential book How to Be a Good Communist, which urged loyalty to the party (and to its chairman) above all.

It is easy to write about Mao as a sole ruler whose orders were never resisted. The historian Jonathan Spence and the Edexcel Paper 3 examiner reports both warn against this. Liu Shaoqi was the formal President from 1959, Zhou Enlai ran the state machinery as Premier, and Peng Dehuai commanded the army in Korea. Mao’s authority over policy decisions was real but never total — later in this unit, you will see Liu and Deng quietly rolling back Great Leap Forward measures, and Peng Dehuai privately criticising Mao at Lushan in 1959. Strong answers weigh Mao’s authority against the agency of these other figures.

The Structure of the New State

Power in the new People’s Republic ran through three parallel hierarchies. The CCP under its Chairman, Mao, set policy. The State Council, headed by Premier Zhou Enlai, ran the day-to-day government. The People’s Liberation Army, the third pillar, was loyal to the party rather than to the state. Where the three overlapped, the party always came first — senior army officers were also CCP members, and government ministers held party posts. CCP membership was the entry ticket to influence. From around 4.5 million members at liberation in 1949, the party grew rapidly: by 1957 it had over 12 million members and by 1976 around 35 million.

At the village level, this meant a CCP danwei (work unit) or party committee that decided who got food rations, work assignments, schooling, and even permission to marry. Mass party membership and democratic centralism therefore did more than fill bureaucratic posts — they reached into ordinary life. The party did not simply govern the state; it became the state.

The Sino-Soviet Treaty, February 1950

In December 1949 Mao travelled to Moscow — his first journey outside China — for two months of difficult talks with Stalin. The result, signed in February 1950, was the Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship, Alliance and Mutual Assistance. The USSR promised $300 million of credit, sent around 10,000 advisers and engineers across the 1950s, and helped China build the heavy industry the First Five-Year Plan would require. The price was steep: most aid was in the form of loans, the Soviets controlled certain joint ventures, and Mao left Moscow privately resenting Stalin’s coolness.

Key Fact

Signed in February 1950, the Sino-Soviet Treaty brought China around $300 million in Soviet credit, c.10,000 Soviet advisers and engineers, and the political backing of Stalin’s USSR. It anchored the new PRC in the communist bloc and underwrote the First Five-Year Plan.

Why China Entered the Korean War

In June 1950, communist North Korea invaded the south. United Nations forces under American command pushed the North Korean army back to the Chinese border by October. Mao’s decision to send around 250,000 Chinese soldiers — officially called the ‘Chinese People’s Volunteers’ under Marshal Peng Dehuai — was made at meetings of the Politburo in October 1950. Several factors weighed in:

  • A US-occupied Korea on China’s north-eastern border was a strategic threat — especially with American forces also in Taiwan and Japan.
  • Stalin urged intervention but, crucially, made it Mao’s choice; this was not simply Soviet orders.
  • The Korean War gave Mao a way to prove the PLA’s worth on the world stage and reinforce his claim to leadership of the global communist movement.

Even though Korea is a foreign war, examiners reward students who can link it back to domestic politics in China. The war fed three things at home. First, propaganda — the ‘Resist America, Aid Korea’ campaign rallied patriotism around the new regime and made dissent dangerous. Second, repression — the simultaneous campaign against ‘counter-revolutionaries’ (1950–52) used wartime urgency to justify the execution of an estimated 700,000–2 million people accused of links to the GMD or to imperialism. Third, debt — military costs to the USSR became loans Mao would still be repaying in the late 1950s, fuelling his eventual break with Khrushchev. By the armistice in July 1953, China had lost between 180,000 and 400,000 dead but emerged with the prestige of having fought the United States to a stalemate.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Mao’s authority rested on Marxism-Leninism adapted to peasant China (the ‘mass line’), democratic centralism, and a growing personality cult — but he still had to manage senior figures like Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai.
  • The new state ran through three pillars — CCP, government and PLA — with the party always on top; mass membership reached down to village danwei.
  • The 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty anchored the PRC in the communist bloc; Mao’s decision to enter the Korean War was his own and used to consolidate the regime at home.

lessons.title: Terror, the Three and Five Antis, and the Hundred Flowers, 1951-57
lessons.description: Mass campaigns, denunciations, and a brief opening for criticism that ended in purge.
lessons.content_html:
Terror as a Tool of Government

By 1951, the People’s Republic was less than two years old. Mao’s government had won the civil war, intervened in Korea and signed the alliance with Stalin — but inside China, GMD networks, secret societies, religious groups and remnants of the urban capitalist class were still everywhere. Between 1950 and 1957, the CCP responded with a sequence of mass campaigns: open terror against ‘counter-revolutionaries’, the Three Antis and Five Antis movements, and the very brief opening of the Hundred Flowers. Each campaign worked by a similar method — public denunciation, mass meetings, struggle sessions — and each ended by tightening party control.

Key Fact

Between 1950 and 1952 the CCP’s campaign against ‘counter-revolutionaries’ killed an estimated 700,000 to 2 million people. Mao himself spoke of executing about one in a thousand — deliberate state policy, not random violence.

The Mass Terror, 1950–52

The campaign against counter-revolutionaries opened in February 1951 and ran alongside the Korean War. The official targets were former GMD officials, secret-society members, ‘bandits’ in the south-west, religious leaders and anyone accused of links to imperialism. In practice, local cadres met quotas: each county was expected to identify a set proportion of ‘enemies’. Suspects were paraded before struggle sessions — large public meetings where they were denounced, made to confess, beaten or made to wear placards. Many were executed publicly to make the lesson visible.

Terror was not the only tool. The CCP also built the laogai — a network of forced-labour camps modelled partly on the Soviet Gulag. By the mid-1950s the laogai held millions of prisoners working on canals, railways, farms and mines. The system became one of the regime’s permanent features, run by the Ministry of Public Security and combining punishment with cheap labour for the new state.

The Three Antis Campaign, 1951

In late 1951 the focus turned inward, onto party officials. Mao launched the Three Antis against corruption, waste and bureaucracy. The targets were inside the system: officials taking bribes, units padding their accounts, cadres shielded from criticism by paperwork. Workers were encouraged to put up ‘big-character posters’ (handwritten denunciations pinned in public) accusing their superiors. Around 4,500,000 government employees were investigated. Most were rebuked or demoted; an estimated 4,500 were executed. The campaign showed the urban population that the CCP would discipline its own — and reminded officials that nobody was untouchable.

The Five Antis Campaign, 1952

The Five Antis followed in early 1952 and turned the same machinery on the urban capitalist class. Its targets were bribery, tax evasion, theft of state property, cheating on government contracts and leaking state economic intelligence. Tens of thousands of business owners were paraded through struggle sessions, especially in Shanghai. Many were forced to pay heavy fines, hand their factories to the state in part, or simply leave the country. Reliable estimates suggest at least several hundred thousand were affected and several thousand committed suicide rather than face denunciation. The economic effect was profound: by 1956, almost all private industry and commerce had been absorbed into the state or into ‘joint state-private’ enterprises.

Because the Three and Five Antis sit in the long shadow of the famine and the Cultural Revolution, students sometimes treat them as small clean-up operations. They were nothing of the sort. They involved struggle sessions, public denunciations, suicides and the political destruction of the urban capitalist class as a force in Chinese life. Strong answers stress that by 1956 the bourgeoisie that had run the cities was gone — that mattered for everything Mao did next, from the First Five-Year Plan to the Hundred Flowers.

The Hundred Flowers Campaign, 1956–57

In May 1956, Mao adapted a phrase from a classical poem: ‘Let a hundred flowers bloom, let a hundred schools of thought contend.’ He invited intellectuals — writers, scientists, professors, journalists — to criticise the party and propose reforms. Several factors lay behind the move. Stalin had died in 1953, and Khrushchev’s ‘Secret Speech’ of February 1956 attacked Stalin’s personality cult; Mao did not want a Chinese version of de-Stalinisation imposed on him. Hungary’s 1956 uprising frightened the whole communist bloc into thinking about safety valves. Mao also believed the bulk of intellectuals — many trained before 1949 — were now safely loyal and could be trusted with limited debate.

The first response was muted. Most intellectuals were cautious. Then in early 1957 Mao gave a much sharper speech, On the Correct Handling of Contradictions Among the People, urging open criticism. From May 1957 onwards, criticism poured in. Posters demanded an end to one-party rule. The student-aged writer Lin Xiling attacked Marxism. The literary editor Hu Feng (already arrested in 1955) became a symbol of intellectuals who had been crushed. Mao was reportedly stunned by the volume.

Mao later claimed he had ‘lured snakes from their holes’ — that the Hundred Flowers had always been a trap. Many CCP-published accounts repeat this. Western historians take a more divided view. Frank Dikötter (The Tragedy of Liberation) and Jonathan Spence (The Search for Modern China) both argue that the early stages were probably a genuine reform — that Mao expected mild criticism, was alarmed by the volume, and reframed the campaign as a trap once it had ended. The historiography is contested. Top-band answers acknowledge both views rather than collapsing the campaign into a single story.

The Anti-Rightist Campaign, June 1957

In June 1957 the door slammed shut. Mao now declared the criticism a plot by ‘rightists’, and Deng Xiaoping was put in charge of the response. Around 500,000 people were labelled rightists between June 1957 and 1958. Many lost their jobs, were demoted, sent to laogai camps, or rusticated to the countryside — sometimes for the next twenty years. The intellectual class as a critical voice was effectively destroyed for a generation. The result mattered for what came next: when Mao launched the Great Leap Forward in 1958, almost no senior figure was willing to challenge it.

Key Fact

The Anti-Rightist Campaign of 1957–58 labelled around 500,000 intellectuals ‘rightists’. It silenced expert criticism, removed a generation of cautious voices from public life, and cleared the political space for the Great Leap Forward of 1958.

Use specific period vocabulary (Hundred Flowers, Anti-Rightist, struggle session, laogai, big-character poster) to lock in SPaG marks where they are available.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1950–52 terror against ‘counter-revolutionaries’ killed 700,000–2 million people; the laogai system of forced-labour camps became permanent.
  • The Three Antis (1951, against officials) and Five Antis (1952, against the urban capitalist class) used struggle sessions to discipline the bureaucracy and absorb private business into the state.
  • The Hundred Flowers Campaign (1956–57) opened a brief space for criticism — whether trap or genuine reform is contested — and ended in the Anti-Rightist purge of c.500,000 intellectuals, clearing the way for the Great Leap Forward.

lessons.title: Land Reform and Agricultural Cooperation, 1949-57
lessons.description: From smashing the landlords to forcing the peasants into ever-larger collective farms.
lessons.content_html:
Why Land Came First

When Mao Zedong proclaimed the People’s Republic in October 1949, roughly 80% of Chinese people lived in the countryside. The CCP had won the Civil War partly by promising the peasants land. The 1950 Agrarian Reform Law turned that promise into policy — but the peasants who received land in 1950 only owned it for about four to six years. By 1956 nearly all rural land had been pooled into cooperatives, and by 1958 it would be absorbed into the people’s communes. Land reform was therefore a single, staged process from private ownership to full collectivisation, not a one-off gift.

Key Fact

The 1950 Agrarian Reform Law sorted every rural household into four classes — landlords, rich peasants, middle peasants and poor peasants. Landlords lost everything; rich peasants kept what they farmed themselves; middle peasants were left alone; poor peasants received the redistributed land.

The 1950 Agrarian Reform Law

The law was drafted by Liu Shaoqi and passed on 30 June 1950. It abolished ‘feudal exploitation’ and ordered the confiscation of all land owned by landlords. The land, plus farm tools and surplus grain, was redistributed to landless and poor peasants. Around 300 million peasants received roughly 47 million hectares of land in the four years that followed. Each household was assigned a class label that would follow them — and their children — for the rest of the Mao era.

The classification process was deliberately public and brutal. CCP work teams arrived in each village and called ‘speak bitterness’ meetings, in which peasants were urged to denounce their former landlords for cruelty and exploitation. Many denunciations led to beatings and execution. Estimates of landlord deaths between 1950 and 1952 range from 1 to 2 million — some by formal trial, many by mob violence with cadre approval. Mao explicitly defended the bloodshed: ‘A revolution is not a dinner party.’ The class war was meant to bind the peasants to the CCP through shared guilt as well as shared gain.

Mutual Aid Teams, 1951–52

Even before redistribution finished, the CCP began encouraging peasants to pool their work. Five to ten households would form a Mutual Aid Team, sharing labour, draught animals and tools at busy times of the year. Land and animals remained privately owned. By the end of 1952 around 40% of peasant households were in some form of mutual aid arrangement. The Mutual Aid Teams were genuinely popular — small enough to feel familiar, and an obvious efficiency gain on tiny family plots.

Lower-Stage and Higher-Stage Cooperatives, 1953–56

Lower-stage cooperatives followed in 1953–54. Around 30 to 50 households pooled land into a single farm; peasants kept formal ownership and were paid both for the labour they did and for the land they brought in. Higher-stage cooperatives, modelled on Soviet collective farms, came next. They contained 200 to 300 households, and the land itself became the collective property of the cooperative — private ownership was effectively abolished. Payment was now strictly by labour. By the end of 1956, around 96% of peasant households had been pushed into higher-stage cooperatives.

Students often assume the 1950 redistribution gave peasants permanent ownership. The reality was sharper — private ownership lasted at most four to six years before being absorbed by the higher-stage cooperatives of 1955–56, then by the people’s communes of 1958. The point of the redistribution was political, not economic: it broke the rural elite and created peasant gratitude to the CCP. Top-band answers spell out this staged sequence rather than presenting land reform as a single event.

The ‘Socialist High Tide’, 1955

Mao’s personal acceleration of cooperation came in his July 1955 speech ‘On the Question of Agricultural Cooperation’, often called the ‘Socialist High Tide’ speech. He attacked cautious officials — including Deng Zihui, head of the Rural Work Department — who wanted a slower, voluntary timetable. Mao argued the masses were ready and that timid leadership was the obstacle. Liu Shaoqi had until then sided with the slower approach. Once Mao spoke, the central plan was rewritten: higher-stage cooperatives that had been targeted for 1960 were to be universal by 1957.

The shift from voluntary to enforced cooperation was driven by several factors. Mao believed cooperatives would raise grain output to feed industry under the First Five-Year Plan. He also feared a return of rich-peasant power if private farming was allowed to consolidate. The earlier Gao Gang affair (1953–54), in which a senior planner was purged, had reinforced Mao’s authority over rural policy. By December 1956 the ‘High Tide’ was complete — ahead of the official schedule and well beyond what most peasants had been asked to accept.

Western historians often compare Chinese collectivisation with Stalin’s in the USSR. Frank Dikötter (The Tragedy of Liberation) and Jonathan Spence (The Search for Modern China) both stress that the Chinese version was at first more cautious — staged through Mutual Aid Teams and lower-stage cooperatives — before Mao’s 1955 speech accelerated it. CCP-orthodox accounts emphasise voluntary peasant enthusiasm; the revisionist Anglophone view stresses cadre quotas and pressure. Mobo Gao’s The Battle for China’s Past notes that early cooperation did improve irrigation and small-scale infrastructure. Top-band answers acknowledge that the early stages were genuinely popular and that the 1955–56 acceleration was where the coercion arrived.

Why It Mattered for What Came Next

By the end of 1956, China had collective land ownership in all but name. Mao now had a rural structure he believed could be pushed further — into the people’s communes of August 1958 and the Great Leap Forward. Liu Shaoqi’s caution about pace had been overruled. Deng Zihui had been sidelined. The intellectual class would be silenced months later in the Anti-Rightist purge. The political space for a vast experiment in agriculture had been cleared — and the famine that followed in 1959–62 was rooted in the structures put in place between 1950 and 1956.

Key Fact

The sequence was: 1950 redistribution to poor peasants, 1951–52 voluntary Mutual Aid Teams, 1953–54 lower-stage cooperatives (private ownership retained), 1955–56 higher-stage cooperatives (collective ownership). The 1958 communes followed directly from this base.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions on land reform, examiners reward students who treat 1950–56 as a single staged process rather than a single event. Be precise on dates and on who pushed for caution (Liu Shaoqi, Deng Zihui) versus who pushed for acceleration (Mao at the ‘Socialist High Tide’ in July 1955). Use period vocabulary — speak bitterness, mutual aid team, higher-stage cooperative — to lock in SPaG marks where they are available, and weigh the views of revisionist (Dikötter, Spence) and sympathetic (Mobo Gao) historians rather than dismissing either on bias alone.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The 1950 Agrarian Reform Law confiscated landlord land and redistributed it to roughly 300 million peasants, with 1–2 million landlords killed in the process.
  • Peasant ownership was a brief stage — Mutual Aid Teams (1951–52), lower-stage cooperatives (1953–54) and higher-stage cooperatives (1955–56) absorbed the land within six years.
  • Mao’s July 1955 ‘Socialist High Tide’ speech overruled cautious figures like Liu Shaoqi and Deng Zihui, accelerating collectivisation and clearing the way for the 1958 communes.

lessons.title: The First Five-Year Plan, 1953-57
lessons.description: Soviet engineers, steel mills and the building of a Chinese industrial base.
lessons.content_html:
Why Mao Wanted Industry Fast

When the People’s Republic was founded in 1949, China was overwhelmingly agricultural. Industrial output was a fraction of the United States or the Soviet Union, and most modern factories had been wrecked by the Sino-Japanese War or the Civil War. The Korean War (1950–53) made the gap impossible to ignore: Chinese soldiers fought a modern American army with First World War-era equipment. Mao concluded that the new state had to industrialise quickly — both to defend itself and to demonstrate that communism could deliver. The result was the First Five-Year Plan, launched in 1953 and inspired directly by Stalin’s Soviet model.

Key Fact

The Soviet Union supplied around 156 ‘gift’ projects (full factory plans and equipment) and roughly 10,000 advisers to China during the First Five-Year Plan. The aid was the backbone of Chinese industrialisation between 1953 and 1957.

Reasons for the Plan

Several reasons converged. First, defence: the Korean War and the threat of US air power made heavy industry urgent. Second, ideology: the Soviet model treated heavy industry — steel, coal, machine tools, electricity — as the proof and engine of socialism. Third, alliance: the 1950 Sino-Soviet Treaty of Friendship gave China access to Soviet engineers, blueprints and credit on favourable terms. Fourth, prestige: catching up with the imperial powers had been a Chinese political obsession since 1842, and the CCP wanted to deliver where the Qing and the GMD had failed.

The plan was substantially designed by Soviet planners and run on the Chinese side by Premier Zhou Enlai, finance specialist Chen Yun and Liu Shaoqi. Mao approved the plan but did not author it — a fact that would matter when he later launched the Great Leap Forward partly as a reaction against the Soviet model.

Targets and Soviet Aid

The Plan set very specific targets. By 1957, steel output was to rise from c.1.3 million tonnes to c.4.1 million tonnes; coal from c.66 million to c.113 million tonnes; electricity generation roughly to double. Around 58% of state investment went into heavy industry; consumer goods and agriculture were squeezed to pay for it. The Soviet contribution arrived in the form of gift projects — full plans for steel mills (Anshan in Manchuria, Wuhan, Baotou), machine-tool factories, power stations and lorry plants. Soviet engineers and managers worked alongside Chinese counterparts; thousands of Chinese students were trained in Russia.

It is tempting to credit (or blame) Mao for everything that happened in 1950s China, but the First Five-Year Plan was substantially designed by Soviet planners and run by Liu Shaoqi, Zhou Enlai and Chen Yun. Mao approved it and presided over it — but he chafed at depending on the Russians and at the bureaucratic, technical character of Soviet planning. Frank Dikötter argues that the Great Leap Forward of 1958 was partly Mao’s deliberate move away from this Soviet-style technocracy. Strong answers separate Mao’s rhetorical leadership from the actual planners and stress that Mao was uncomfortable in the role of cautious manager.

Successes

Headline industrial output grew by around 118% over the five years — far faster than any previous Chinese government had achieved. New industrial cities took shape: Anshan became the country’s steel capital, Wuhan a heavy-engineering hub, Changchun the centre of the new lorry industry. The urban industrial workforce expanded from c.6 million in 1952 to c.10 million by 1957. The state-run danwei system gave urban workers housing, healthcare, ration coupons and pensions in return for political loyalty. For the workers inside the system, life genuinely improved.

The Plan also delivered infrastructure that would matter for decades: rail extensions into the south-west, a doubling of installed electrical capacity, and the country’s first wave of indigenous machine-tool production. Most headline industrial targets were met or exceeded by the end of 1957.

Failures and Strains

The successes came at real cost. Agriculture was deliberately squeezed to feed the cities and pay for imported equipment, contributing to rural discontent that fed Mao’s acceleration of collectivisation in 1955–56. Consumer goods were scarce; clothing, household items and most food beyond the basic ration were rare. Quality control was uneven — Soviet-built plants worked, but local imitations frequently produced low-grade output. Bureaucratic planning bred its own waste: factory managers padded reports to please planners.

There was a deeper political strain. Dependence on the USSR sat uncomfortably with Mao’s revolutionary self-image. Stalin’s death in March 1953 and Khrushchev’s 1956 ‘Secret Speech’ attacking Stalin’s personality cult unsettled the Sino-Soviet relationship. Soviet aid was generous in scale but was treated by Beijing as a debt to be repaid in goods, not a free gift. Mao began to look for a Chinese alternative model — one that relied on the masses rather than on Soviet engineers.

CCP-orthodox accounts treat the First Five-Year Plan as a clear success and the high point of co-operation with the USSR. Sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao point to the lasting infrastructure base it built — rail, electricity, steel cities — which underpinned later Chinese growth. Revisionist historians (Frank Dikötter, Jonathan Spence) accept the headline output figures but stress the squeeze on agriculture, the inflated reporting from below, and the political tensions with Moscow. Top-band answers acknowledge both: that the Plan delivered an industrial base, and that it set up the very conflicts — over peasants, planning style and Soviet aid — that Mao would resolve by smashing the model in 1958.

Key Fact

Despite hitting most industrial targets, the First Five-Year Plan squeezed agriculture, kept consumer goods scarce, and made China uncomfortably dependent on c.10,000 Soviet advisers. By 1957 these strains had pushed Mao to abandon the model and launch the Great Leap Forward.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions on the First Five-Year Plan, examiners reward students who weigh successes (industrial output, new cities, infrastructure) against failures (agriculture squeezed, consumer goods scarce, dependence on the USSR) and link both to what came next. Use specific period vocabulary — danwei, gift project, heavy industry — to lock in SPaG marks. Avoid the trap of treating headline tonnage figures as full success without examining quality, reporting accuracy and rural cost.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The First Five-Year Plan (1953–57) was modelled on Soviet practice, designed largely by Soviet planners, and run on the Chinese side by Zhou Enlai, Chen Yun and Liu Shaoqi.
  • Soviet aid — c.156 ‘gift’ projects and c.10,000 advisers — built new industrial cities (Anshan, Wuhan, Baotou) and roughly doubled industrial output, with most headline targets met by 1957.
  • The Plan squeezed agriculture and consumer goods, depended uncomfortably on the USSR, and pushed Mao towards the more radical, mass-mobilising Great Leap Forward of 1958.

lessons.title: The Great Leap Forward, 1958-62
lessons.description: Communes, backyard furnaces and the gulf between Mao’s targets and reality.
lessons.content_html:
A Different Kind of Plan

By 1957 the First Five-Year Plan had built steel cities and factories — but Mao Zedong was uncomfortable. The plan had relied on Soviet engineers, technocrats and bureaucratic targets. After Khrushchev’s ‘Secret Speech’ of 1956 attacked Stalin’s personality cult, Mao distrusted the Soviet model more than ever. He wanted a Chinese revolution that mobilised the masses, not one that depended on Russian advisers. The result was the second Five-Year Plan, launched in 1958 and quickly renamed the Great Leap Forward. Its slogan was ‘catch up with Britain in 15 years’. Its result was the worst peacetime famine in modern history.

Key Fact

By the end of 1958, around 26,000 people’s communes had absorbed roughly 99% of rural households. Each commune averaged 5,000 households and combined farming, small industry, schools, militia training and a communal mess hall.

Mao’s Reasons

Mao’s reasons were ideological as much as economic. The Soviet model relied on bureaucratic engineers; Mao believed China’s revolutionary masses, properly mobilised, could leap past it. He wanted to overtake Britain in steel within fifteen years, prove the superiority of Chinese socialism, and reassert his own authority over rivals like Liu Shaoqi who had run the more cautious First Plan. The 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign had silenced the intellectuals who might have raised objections, and the political space for an enormous experiment was open.

There was also a practical aim: by squeezing more grain and labour out of the countryside, Mao hoped to fund industry without continued reliance on Soviet credit. The peasants had already been moved into higher-stage cooperatives by the end of 1956, so the structural step to communes was small. Mao called for ‘walking on two legs’ — modern industry in the cities and mass effort in the villages, both at the same time.

The People’s Communes

From August 1958, higher-stage cooperatives were merged into people’s communes. Private farming was abolished. Even the small private plots permitted in 1956 were taken back. Family cooking was banned in favour of communal mess halls (around 3.4 million across China by mid-1959), where peasants ate without paying for meals so long as the harvest held. Communes ran their own primary schools, clinics, repair shops and militia. Women were enlisted into mass labour; childcare was collective.

Productivity was supposed to rise through scale and through what Mao called ‘people’s war’ methods on the farm. Older peasant practices were dismissed as superstition. The methods of the Soviet pseudo-scientist Lysenkoism — deep ploughing of three feet, planting seeds three to four times closer than normal, refusing fertiliser — were imposed nationwide. The crops planted under these rules either grew too thickly to ripen, or rotted in waterlogged fields. Inflated reports passed up the system claimed huge harvests; the central state set procurement quotas based on those false figures.

Backyard Steel

The most famous symbol of the Leap was the backyard steel furnace. From August 1958 every commune was required to produce steel. Around 60 million peasants were diverted from the harvest to feed small clay or brick furnaces with scrap iron, household pots and kettles. The output was almost worthless — Frank Dikötter calls it ‘tofu-dreg metal’, brittle and unusable in any factory. Yet the campaign continued because the political signal — that the masses, not engineers, could industrialise China — mattered more than the economics. The diversion of peasant labour from the fields was a key contributor to the famine that followed.

Students sometimes treat the Great Leap as a well-intentioned plan that hit unexpected problems. The targets were physically impossible from the start — doubling steel output in a year, planting wheat at four times normal density, abolishing private farming overnight. The structure of communal mess halls and backyard steel was always going to fail. Strong answers stress that the policy combined an unworkable agricultural science with an unworkable industrial method, and that the cost was visible to local cadres long before Beijing admitted it.

The Lushan Conference, July–August 1959

By 1959 the strain showed. Marshal Peng Dehuai, hero of the Korean War, returned from a tour of his home province of Hunan with first-hand reports of starvation. At the Lushan Conference (2 July to 16 August 1959) he gave Mao a private letter setting out his concerns: peasants going hungry, exaggerated grain figures, ‘petty-bourgeois fanaticism’ in policy. Mao circulated the letter to the whole conference and treated it as a personal attack. Peng was denounced, stripped of his role as Defence Minister, and replaced by Lin Biao — who would build the Mao cult that came next.

Lushan mattered for two reasons. First, it reasserted Mao’s personal authority over policy at the moment when policy was failing. Second, it made future criticism politically lethal. Even as the famine deepened in 1960–61, no senior figure inside the CCP was willing to challenge Mao directly. The Leap was eased rather than reversed; the communes survived, though private plots quietly returned in many areas under Liu Shaoqi’s recovery measures.

Western historians disagree on where the Great Leap came from. Frank Dikötter (Mao’s Great Famine) argues for a top-down policy of personal command by Mao, with the Lushan Conference as the moment he chose to prolong rather than reverse the disaster. Roderick MacFarquhar emphasises the role of provincial cadres pushing inflated figures upwards to please Beijing. Yang Jisheng’s Tombstone blends both. Mobo Gao argues that the Leap had genuine local successes — irrigation works, small-scale industry, women in mass employment — and that the famine, terrible as it was, has been politicised in Western writing. Top-band answers acknowledge that the Leap was ordered by Mao and amplified by cadres, and that the real argument is over how much human cost was inevitable.

Key Fact

The Great Leap built failure into its design: communal mess halls destroyed peasant incentives, Lysenkoist farming wrecked the 1959 harvest, and 60 million peasants were pulled from fields to backyard furnaces. At Lushan in July 1959, Mao chose to purge his critic Peng Dehuai rather than reverse course.

Use specific period vocabulary — commune, mess hall, Lushan, Lysenkoism, Great Leap — to lock in SPaG marks. Avoid presenting the Lushan Conference as a moment of climbdown; Mao doubled down and removed the critic.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) replaced cooperatives with c.26,000 people’s communes covering c.99% of rural households, abolishing private farming and family cooking.
  • Backyard steel furnaces, Lysenkoist agriculture and inflated reporting combined to wreck the harvest, while c.60 million peasants were diverted from farming to steel.
  • At the Lushan Conference (1959) Mao purged Peng Dehuai for criticising the Leap, replaced him with Lin Biao, and prolonged the policy — setting up the famine of 1959–62.

lessons.title: The Great Famine and Recovery under Liu and Deng, 1959-65
lessons.description: Tens of millions die; pragmatists pull the country back while Mao retreats from day-to-day rule.
lessons.content_html:
A Famine Made by Policy

Between 1959 and 1962, China suffered the largest peacetime loss of life in modern history. Historians’ estimates of the dead range from around 15 million to 45 million. The dominant cause was not weather. It was a chain of policy decisions: the people’s communes of 1958, communal mess halls that ate through grain reserves, Lysenkoist farming methods that wrecked the 1959 harvest, the diversion of around 60 million peasants from fields to backyard steel, and forced state procurement quotas based on inflated reports. The CCP for decades called the period ‘three years of natural disasters’. The historiography of the past thirty years — Frank Dikötter, Yang Jisheng, Roderick MacFarquhar — has dismantled that framing.

Key Fact

Historians estimate 15–45 million deaths in the Great Famine of 1958–62. Frank Dikötter argues for c.45 million (Mao’s Great Famine, 2010) and Yang Jisheng for c.36 million (Tombstone). The CCP’s long-standing label ‘three years of natural disasters’ framed the famine as weather-driven; modern scholarship treats it as policy-driven.

Causes of the Famine

The famine had multiple causes layered over the same harvest. The first was structural: the communes destroyed peasant incentives to produce. Private plots were banned; communal mess halls served the same meals to everyone whether they worked or not. The second was scientific: grain procurement quotas were set on the basis of inflated yield figures sent up from local cadres who feared denunciation if they reported the truth. Provinces sent grain to the cities and to the export market while villages starved.

The third was personal. After Peng Dehuai was purged at the Lushan Conference in July 1959, no senior CCP figure was willing to challenge Mao directly. Procurement quotas were maintained or raised in 1959 and 1960 even as the harvest collapsed. The fourth was external: in July 1960 Khrushchev withdrew the c.10,000 Soviet advisers in the wake of the deepening Sino-Soviet split, removing technical help at the worst moment. Weather was a factor — floods and drought in 1960 hit some provinces hard — but the policy framework determined who lived and died.

For decades the CCP framed the Great Famine as weather-driven. Modern historians disagree. Frank Dikötter (Mao’s Great Famine) and Yang Jisheng (Tombstone) argue that the structures of the Great Leap — communes, mess halls, banned private farming, Lysenkoism, inflated reporting and forced procurement — were the dominant cause. Weather mattered in 1960 but cannot explain why grain continued to be exported, why procurement was maintained after Lushan, or why the famine peaked in provinces with the most aggressive cadres rather than the worst weather. Strong answers identify the famine as a policy disaster amplified, not caused, by weather.

The Sino-Soviet Split, July 1960

The deteriorating relationship with Moscow reached its breaking point in 1960. Mao’s ideological attacks on Khrushchev’s ‘peaceful coexistence’ with the West, and Khrushchev’s contempt for the Great Leap, led to the formal withdrawal of Soviet advisers in July. Half-completed projects from the First Five-Year Plan stalled. Loans had to be repaid in grain at exactly the moment the famine was at its worst. The Sino-Soviet split confirmed Mao’s view that China should rely on its own efforts, but it removed an external check that might have moderated the disaster.

The 7,000 Cadres Conference, January 1962

By late 1961 the famine could no longer be denied inside the leadership. At the 7,000 Cadres Conference in January 1962 — the largest internal meeting in CCP history — Liu Shaoqi stood up and said publicly that the famine was ‘30% natural disaster, 70% man-made’. Mao made a partial self-criticism. Power began to shift. Liu Shaoqi, as President of the PRC since 1959, took daily charge of the economy together with Deng Xiaoping, who was General Secretary of the CCP. Mao retreated to a less operational role — but never forgave the moment. He later told Edgar Snow he had begun, even then, to plan a second cultural revolution.

Recovery under Liu and Deng, 1962–65

Liu and Deng’s recovery measures are best summarised by the slogan sanzi yibao — ‘three freedoms and one contract’. Private plots were restored, free rural markets reopened, small private sideline industries were allowed, and household production contracts let families farm a piece of communal land in return for delivering a fixed quota. Communal mess halls were quietly closed. Industry was rebalanced: backyard steel was abandoned, fertiliser plants were built, and Soviet-style machine-tool factories rebuilt the urban industrial base. Chen Yun returned as the leading economic planner.

By 1965 grain output had recovered to roughly pre-Leap levels. Industrial output exceeded 1957 levels. Famine deaths ended. The recovery was framed in the language of socialism — Liu and Deng never proposed liberal markets — but for Mao it looked like surrender. He saw Liu and Deng as ‘capitalist roaders’ restoring the old order under a new label. The political conflict that recovery created became the launching pad for the Cultural Revolution of 1966.

Students often present Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping as anti-Mao throughout. The truth is more layered. Both backed the Great Leap in 1958. Both shifted only in 1961–62 once the human cost was undeniable. Their reforms used socialist language — ‘three freedoms’ and ‘one contract’ — not liberal-market language. Frank Dikötter (The Cultural Revolution) reads them as cautious pragmatists, not market reformers. Mobo Gao argues their changes were modest and that even at their height the commune framework remained. Strong answers describe the recovery as a course correction within the socialist framework, not a Western-style liberalisation, and explain why Mao misread it as a counter-revolution.

Key Fact

The recovery slogan sanzi yibao covered: private plots restored, free rural markets, private sideline industries, and household production contracts. By 1965 grain and industrial output had recovered to pre-Leap levels — but Mao saw the policy package as a betrayal that justified the Cultural Revolution.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions on the famine, examiners reward students who treat policy as the dominant cause and weather as a contributing factor, not the other way round. Be precise on dates, figures and named historians (Dikötter c.45 million, Yang Jisheng c.36 million). For questions on Liu and Deng’s recovery, stress that sanzi yibao was a course correction within socialism, not a liberal turn, and link it to Mao’s reaction in 1966. Use period vocabulary — commune, sanzi yibao, capitalist roaders, 7,000 Cadres Conference — to lock in SPaG marks where they are available.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Great Famine of 1958–62 killed an estimated 15–45 million people; modern historians (Dikötter, Yang Jisheng, MacFarquhar) treat it as a policy disaster amplified by weather, not the other way round.
  • At the 7,000 Cadres Conference of January 1962, Liu Shaoqi described the famine as ‘30% natural, 70% man-made’; Mao made a partial self-criticism and stepped back from daily economic management.
  • Liu and Deng’s sanzi yibao reforms (1962–65) restored private plots, free markets and household contracts, and recovered output by 1965 — but set up Mao’s 1966 backlash as the Cultural Revolution.

lessons.title: Origins of the Cultural Revolution, 1962-66
lessons.description: Mao's comeback bid: how Lin Biao's cult and the Socialist Education Movement set up 1966.
lessons.content_html:
Why Did Mao Need a New Revolution?

By 1962, Mao Zedong was the chairman of a victorious party but a defeated policymaker. The Great Leap Forward (1958–62) and the famine that followed had killed at least 15 million people, and the recovery was being run by Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping — not by Mao. Liu’s 1962 ‘Seven Thousand Cadres’ speech blamed the disaster on policy errors ‘30 per cent natural, 70 per cent man-made’. Mao stepped back from day-to-day rule but never accepted that judgement. He believed the party itself had grown soft, ‘capitalist roaders’ were creeping back into power, and that only a new Cultural Revolution could restart the revolution.

Key Fact

Between 1962 and 1966, Mao prepared a comeback against his own party through three linked moves — the Socialist Education Movement to attack rural cadres, Lin Biao’s PLA cult of Mao, and a campaign in education and culture against ‘bourgeois’ thinking.

The Power Struggle: Mao, Liu and Deng

After the Great Leap, Liu Shaoqi (President of the PRC from 1959) and Deng Xiaoping (General Secretary of the CCP) ran the recovery. They scaled back the communes, allowed peasants small private plots, restored material incentives in factories and rebuilt the bureaucracy. Production climbed back. To Mao, however, this looked like the Soviet Union under Khrushchev — the revolution being quietly buried under managers, technicians and bonuses. He began to call Liu ‘China’s Khrushchev’ in private. Deng was accused of treating the party like a card game: ‘black cat or white cat, so long as it catches mice’. Mao’s answer was to widen the political quarrel into a moral one about the soul of communism.

The Socialist Education Movement, 1962–65

The first concrete campaign was the Socialist Education Movement, also called the ‘four cleanups’: clean politics, clean economics, clean organisation, clean ideology. Liu Shaoqi was put in charge. Work teams were sent into villages to root out corrupt accountants and party secretaries. But Mao steadily redirected the campaign upwards. By 1964–65 he was insisting the real enemy was not a few crooked village officials but ‘those in authority taking the capitalist road’ inside the party. Liu and Deng had run the campaign themselves — and now the same campaign was being turned against them.

Students often picture Liu and Deng as bystanders ambushed in 1966. In fact they ran the Socialist Education Movement themselves and supplied much of its language about ‘capitalist roaders’. What they did not anticipate was that Mao would point those same labels at them. Historians like Roderick MacFarquhar argue the four cleanups were the dress rehearsal for the Cultural Revolution — the methods (work teams, denunciation meetings, public confessions) were already in place by 1965, just aimed at lower targets.

Lin Biao and the PLA Cult of Mao

While Liu ran the state, Lin Biao turned the People’s Liberation Army into Mao’s personal political base. Appointed Defence Minister in 1959, Lin replaced Peng Dehuai, the marshal who had been purged at Lushan for criticising the Great Leap. Lin made Mao’s thought the moral spine of military training. In 1964 the PLA published the pocket-sized ‘Quotations from Chairman Mao’ — the Little Red Book — first for soldiers, then for cadres, then nationally. Soldiers were drilled in ‘the three constantly read articles’ (short essays by Mao) and the slogan ‘Learn from the PLA’ was pushed across civilian life. By 1966 the army was loyal to Mao personally, not to the state council or to Liu.

Key Fact

Lin Biao’s 1964 publication of the ‘Quotations from Chairman Mao’ (the Little Red Book) gave the cult of Mao its central scripture. The slogan ‘Learn from the PLA’ pushed military political training into civilian life and prepared the country for mass mobilisation in 1966.

Reform of Education

Mao’s third front was the schools and universities. Examinations were attacked as a way of restoring privilege: a peasant’s son with mud on his boots, Mao argued, was being filtered out by middle-class teachers using bourgeois entrance tests. From 1964 entry to senior schools and universities was tilted towards class background: applicants were classified as ‘red’ (worker, peasant, soldier) or ‘black’ (landlord, rich peasant, capitalist), with the ‘red’ categories favoured. Senior academics were criticised in the press as ‘bourgeois authorities’. The education system that had recruited Liu and Deng’s technocrats was being undermined from below before the Cultural Revolution opened officially.

The Wu Han Affair and the May 16 Notification

The trigger came in November 1965, when the Shanghai propagandist Yao Wenyuan published an attack on a play by the Beijing official Wu Han, ‘Hai Rui Dismissed from Office’. The play described an honest Ming dynasty official sacked for telling the emperor the truth. Mao read it as a coded defence of Peng Dehuai, the marshal he had purged in 1959. The attack on Wu Han widened into an attack on the Beijing party leadership that protected him. On 16 May 1966 the Politburo issued the May 16 Notification, drafted under Mao’s direction. It denounced Liu’s allies as a ‘black gang’ and warned that ‘capitalist roaders’ had infiltrated the party, the army, the government and culture. The notification set up the Cultural Revolution Group around Jiang Qing, Chen Boda and Kang Sheng. The Cultural Revolution was now official.

Was Mao defending the revolution or himself? The orthodox CCP ‘70 per cent right, 30 per cent wrong’ verdict (1981) treats the Cultural Revolution as an honest mistake by an ageing leader. Revisionist Western historians — Frank Dikötter, Jung Chang and Jon Halliday, Roderick MacFarquhar — argue Mao engineered the campaign to destroy rivals who had outflanked him after the Great Leap. Sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao argue that the desire to renew the revolution was genuine, even if the methods were catastrophic. Strong Paper 3 answers acknowledge that the ‘why’ is a contested historical question with different schools of thought, not a settled fact.

Key Takeaways

  • After the Great Leap, Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping ran the recovery and Mao stepped back — but Mao saw the recovery as a betrayal of the revolution and prepared a comeback.
  • Three campaigns from 1962–65 set up 1966: the Socialist Education Movement (which Liu ran but Mao redirected), Lin Biao’s Little Red Book and PLA cult, and the attack on ‘bourgeois’ education.
  • The Wu Han affair (Nov 1965) and the May 16 Notification (1966) launched the Cultural Revolution officially — but historians disagree on whether Mao was defending the revolution or himself.

lessons.title: The Red Guards and the Red Terror, 1966-68
lessons.description: Mao's teenagers attack the 'four olds', tear apart the CCP and slide into factional civil war.
lessons.content_html:
Mao's Mass Movement

In May 1966, the Cultural Revolution Group around Jiang Qing, Chen Boda and Kang Sheng issued the May 16 Notification, warning of ‘capitalist roaders’ inside the party. The directive called on young people to defend the revolution by their own action. The result was the Red Guards — secondary-school and university students, first organised in Beijing on 29 May 1966, then spreading nationwide. They wore red armbands, swore loyalty to Chairman Mao, carried the Little Red Book and attacked anyone they judged to stand for old China. By August Mao was ready to put millions of them on the streets.

Key Fact

Between August and November 1966, Mao reviewed roughly 12 million Red Guards in eight Tiananmen Square rallies. The first, on 18 August 1966, drew about one million teenagers. Free railway travel was provided so students could come from across China.

Mao's Hold on Young People

Why did the young respond so completely? Three reasons mattered. First, Lin Biao’s PLA cult of Mao had filled school curricula since 1964: the ‘three constantly read articles’ and the Little Red Book were already part of daily life. Second, the reform of education had told peasant and worker children that academic exams favoured the bourgeoisie — joining the Red Guards offered a different ladder of merit, based on revolutionary loyalty rather than test scores. Third, on 5 August 1966 Mao published his own big-character poster, ‘Bombard the Headquarters’, telling students that the enemies of the revolution were inside the CCP itself. For teenagers, attacking their teachers and even local party bosses was now rebranded as the highest form of patriotism.

The Four Olds

On 18 August 1966 Lin Biao called from the Tiananmen rostrum for an attack on the four olds: old customs, old culture, old habits and old ideas. In practice this licensed a wave of cultural destruction. Buddhist and Daoist temples were smashed; Christian churches were boarded up; ancestral graves were dug up; classical novels were burned in piles in the street; traditional musical instruments and theatrical costumes were destroyed. Confucius’s tomb at Qufu was desecrated by Beijing Red Guards in November 1966. Names of streets, shops and even people were changed to revolutionary slogans — one Beijing road became ‘Anti-Imperialism Road’. Foreign-style clothing, ‘bourgeois’ haircuts and high heels were cut off in the street.

Students often picture 1966–68 as undirected madness. Frank Dikötter and Roderick MacFarquhar both stress a dual character: the agenda was set top-down, but the violence on the ground became uncontrolled. Mao chose the targets — capitalist roaders, the four olds, intellectuals, ‘black’ class backgrounds. Jiang Qing’s Cultural Revolution Group choreographed the press campaign. But once millions of teenagers were given the licence and the railway tickets, no one in Beijing could control which streets they swept down or which neighbours they denounced. Top-down direction, anarchy on the ground — both at once.

Jiang Qing and the Attack on the CCP

Jiang Qing — Mao’s fourth wife and a former Shanghai actress — turned the Red Guard movement against the CCP itself. As deputy head of the Cultural Revolution Group, she ran the press campaign that named senior officials as ‘capitalist roaders’. Liu Shaoqi was paraded in a dunce cap at a Tsinghua University rally; in October 1966 Lin Biao publicly attacked him at a Politburo work conference. Deng Xiaoping was sent to a Jiangxi tractor factory. Senior teachers and academics were forced to wear placards listing their crimes and stand bent over in the ‘jet plane’ struggle session. Beatings became routine. By the end of 1966 the existing CCP hierarchy was broken; by 1967 entire provincial governments had collapsed.

Cultural Destruction and Human Cost

The cost in lives and culture was enormous. Best estimates from Frank Dikötter and Yang Jisheng put the dead between 1.5 and 1.8 million across the wider Cultural Revolution decade, with most occurring in 1966–68 and again in 1967–71 when the army imposed order. Suicides among intellectuals were common: in Shanghai alone several thousand were recorded in 1966. The writer Lao She drowned himself in a Beijing lake after being beaten at a struggle session. Libraries, museums and family heirlooms were destroyed. Whole categories of people — landlords, rich peasants, counter-revolutionaries, bad elements, rightists — were collectively known as the ‘five black categories’ and treated as enemies whose children were routinely barred from schools and jobs.

The Slide into Anarchy, 1967–68

By early 1967 the movement turned on itself. In the ‘January Storm’ in Shanghai, radical workers and Red Guards seized the city government and declared a ‘Shanghai Commune’. Across China, Red Guards split into rival factions — ‘rebel’ groups attacking established power, ‘royalist’ groups defending it — and then split again. Many seized weapons from PLA depots. By summer 1967 there was open factional warfare in cities like Wuhan, where on 20 July 1967 (the ‘Wuhan Incident’) regional military commanders backed one faction and briefly detained two of Mao’s envoys. Mao now feared the chaos would topple the regime itself. He turned to Lin Biao and the PLA to restore order, beginning the de-mobilisation of the very Red Guards he had unleashed.

The orthodox CCP ‘Resolution on Certain Questions’ (1981) treats the Red Terror as a tragic deviation by an ageing Mao manipulated by Lin Biao and Jiang Qing — a way of preserving Mao’s pre-1956 reputation. Revisionist Western historians like Frank Dikötter and Roderick MacFarquhar argue that Mao deliberately used the Red Guards to destroy rivals he could not defeat through normal CCP channels. Sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao argue that the broader campaign against entrenched bureaucracy had genuine popular support, even as the violence on the ground became indefensible. Strong Paper 3 answers can hold all three readings at once and use them to explain why interpretations differ.

Key Fact

Once Red Guards split into rival factions and seized PLA weapons, Mao’s own movement threatened to bring down the regime. The Wuhan Incident of July 1967 marked the turning point: from late 1967 the PLA was sent in to restore order and rein in the Red Guards.

lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Between August and November 1966, Mao mobilised about 12 million Red Guards across eight Tiananmen rallies; Lin Biao’s ‘Bombard the Headquarters’ speech licensed attacks on the ‘four olds’ and on the CCP itself.
  • Jiang Qing and the Cultural Revolution Group directed the press campaign that purged Liu Shaoqi and Deng Xiaoping; struggle sessions, beatings and cultural destruction marked 1966–67.
  • By 1967–68 Red Guard factions seized PLA weapons and fought each other; the Wuhan Incident pushed Mao to call in the army to restore order.
