lessons.title: Restoring Order: PLA, Lin Biao and the End of the Cultural Revolution, 1968-76
lessons.description: The PLA restores order, Lin Biao falls, and the Gang of Four reach for power before Mao dies.
lessons.content_html:
Calling in the Army

By the summer of 1967, Mao Zedong had a problem of his own making. The Red Guards he had unleashed had splintered into rival factions, looted PLA armouries and turned cities like Wuhan and Shanghai into battlegrounds. The Wuhan Incident of July 1967 showed Mao that even regional military commanders could no longer be trusted to police the chaos. From late 1967 the People’s Liberation Army was sent in to restore order. PLA ‘mass support’ teams entered factories, schools and government offices. Where Red Guard groups refused to disband, the army arrested or shot their leaders. The instrument that had launched the Cultural Revolution — mobilised teenagers — was now the obstacle to controlling it.

Key Fact

From December 1968, Mao launched the ‘Up to the Mountains, Down to the Countryside’ (xiaxiang) campaign. Roughly 17 million urban young people, most of them former Red Guards, were sent to remote villages between 1968 and 1976. The movement that had attacked the CCP was now scattered into the rural fields.

The Purge of the Party Leadership

The PLA imposed order, but the political purges did not stop. In October 1968 the Twelfth Plenum expelled Liu Shaoqi from the CCP and stripped him of all posts. Liu was held without medical care and died of pneumonia in a Kaifeng prison cell in November 1969 — his family was not told for three years. Deng Xiaoping was sent to a tractor factory in Jiangxi but escaped death; his son Pufang was thrown from a Beijing window during the Red Terror and crippled. Most provincial party committees had collapsed; in their place stood ‘revolutionary committees’ chaired by PLA officers. By the Ninth Party Congress in April 1969, the CCP that emerged was a fraction of its 1965 size, dominated by army men and Cultural Revolution radicals.

The Rise and Fall of Lin Biao

At the Ninth Party Congress, Defence Minister Lin Biao was formally written into the new constitution as Mao’s ‘close comrade-in-arms and successor’. It was the high point of his career. It was also the start of his fall. Mao began to suspect Lin of plotting to take power early; the two men quarrelled over the abolition of the post of state chairman in 1970. Then on 13 September 1971, Lin’s Trident jet crashed in the desert of Mongolia, killing him, his wife and his son. The official version — never independently verified — is that he had been fleeing the country after a failed coup, ‘Project 571’, against Mao. Whatever the truth, the affair was a public disaster. The man who had built the cult of Mao was now denounced as a traitor; the Little Red Books had to be reprinted to remove his preface. Mao’s succession plan lay in ruins, and his own health declined sharply afterwards.

By 1971 Mao was visibly ailing — Parkinson’s, motor neurone disease and depression all played a part. The Lin Biao affair shocked him into withdrawal; he barely appeared in public for months. Two rival factions now jostled openly for the succession: the radicals around Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen, who had built their power inside the Cultural Revolution apparatus, and the pragmatists around Premier Zhou Enlai and the rehabilitated Deng Xiaoping. Historians like Frank Dikötter argue that Mao’s control was real but selective: he could still pick winners and losers, but the day-to-day government was no longer his.

Zhou Enlai, Deng Xiaoping and the Four Modernisations

Premier Zhou Enlai, Mao’s closest senior partner since Yan’an, used the post-Lin shock to rebuild government. In February 1972 he hosted President Richard Nixon in Beijing — the opening to the United States that ended China’s isolation. In 1973 he recalled Deng Xiaoping from internal exile and made him Vice Premier. In January 1975 Zhou unveiled the ‘Four Modernisations’ — agriculture, industry, defence, science and technology — the framework for what would later become Deng’s reform era. But Zhou himself was dying of cancer. He died on 8 January 1976. The radicals had blocked the public mourning they feared would become a political demonstration; on 5 April 1976 (the Tiananmen Incident) crowds laid wreaths to Zhou and clashed with police. Deng was blamed and purged for a second time.

The Gang of Four

Through Mao’s last years, four Cultural Revolution radicals based in Shanghai dominated culture, propaganda and education: Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen — the Gang of Four. Jiang Qing’s ‘eight model operas’ were the only theatre permitted; films, books and music outside the model were banned. Schools and universities still operated on the ‘red’ class background system, and the gaokao (university entrance exam) had been suspended since 1966. The radicals attacked Deng under the slogan ‘Criticise Deng and the Right Deviationist Wind’ in early 1976. They expected to inherit power on Mao’s death. They were wrong.

Was the Cultural Revolution ended by the army in 1968, by Mao’s declining health from 1971, by Zhou Enlai’s rebuilding from 1972–75, or only by Mao’s death and the arrest of the Gang of Four in 1976? The orthodox CCP ‘Resolution’ (1981) frames the Cultural Revolution as ‘ten years of chaos’ (1966–76), keeping it as a single block. Revisionist historians like Frank Dikötter and Roderick MacFarquhar argue the violent ‘mass phase’ ended in 1968, but the political purges and cultural restrictions continued until Mao’s death. Sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao stress positive social changes — rural healthcare, literacy — that survived into the 1970s. Strong Paper 3 answers name a school of thought rather than just ‘some historians say’.

The Death of Mao and the Arrest of the Gang of Four

Mao died on 9 September 1976, aged 82. His chosen successor was not a radical but a compromise figure — Hua Guofeng, an industrial Hunanese cadre Mao had promoted in 1971. Hua had a Mao quotation as his title to power: ‘With you in charge, I am at ease’. Within a month, on 6 October 1976, Hua acted. Backed by veteran marshal Ye Jianying and the Beijing garrison, he had the Gang of Four arrested at a Politburo meeting. Their show trial in 1980–81 sentenced Jiang Qing to death, suspended for two years and later commuted to life imprisonment; she committed suicide in 1991. Hua himself was outmanoeuvred by Deng Xiaoping during 1978–80, who returned to power and launched the reform era. The Cultural Revolution was over.

Key Fact

Four turning points ended the Cultural Revolution: PLA restoration of order from 1967–68; the Lin Biao affair (Sept 1971) which broke Mao’s succession plan; Zhou Enlai’s Four Modernisations (1975); and the arrest of the Gang of Four (Oct 1976) by Hua Guofeng one month after Mao’s death.

For interpretation questions, examiners reward students who can name the rival factions (radicals around Jiang Qing versus pragmatists around Zhou and Deng) and explain why historians writing under the orthodox CCP line, the revisionist Western school (Dikötter, MacFarquhar) or the sympathetic line (Mobo Gao) reach different verdicts on Mao’s last years. Use precise vocabulary — xiaxiang, Gang of Four, Four Modernisations, Tiananmen Incident — to lock in SPaG marks on the 20-mark question.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • From late 1967 the PLA was sent in to disband the Red Guards; Liu Shaoqi was expelled from the CCP in 1968 and died in detention in 1969; the xiaxiang campaign sent c.17 million urban youth to the countryside.
  • Lin Biao, named Mao’s successor in 1969, died in a plane crash in Mongolia in September 1971 after an alleged coup — breaking Mao’s succession plan and damaging the cult.
  • Zhou Enlai recalled Deng Xiaoping in 1973 and announced the Four Modernisations in 1975; on Mao’s death in September 1976, Hua Guofeng arrested the Gang of Four within a month, ending the Cultural Revolution.

lessons.title: Communist Control: Propaganda, Censorship and the Cult of Mao
lessons.description: The Little Red Book, mass propaganda and laogai labour camps — how Mao’s China policed the mind.
lessons.content_html:
A State That Reached Into Every Mind

By the mid-1950s the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) ruled c.600 million people, most of them illiterate peasants spread across vast countryside. Direct rule by police alone was impossible. Instead Mao Zedong built a system of propaganda, censorship and surveillance that aimed to reach every village square, every factory and every dinner table. The aim was not just to silence opposition but to produce loyal citizens who would internalise the party line and police themselves. By the late 1960s, posters of Mao hung in railway stations, classrooms and family homes; loudspeakers piped political broadcasts into village streets; and a billion copies of the Little Red Book had been printed.

Key Fact

Defence Minister Lin Biao first issued the Little Red Book to the People’s Liberation Army in 1964. By the early 1970s over a billion copies had been printed — one of the largest print runs of any book in history.

Mass Propaganda

CCP propaganda worked at every level. Posters in bright colours showed Mao surrounded by smiling peasants and soldiers; radio broadcasts and street loudspeakers piped revolutionary songs and party slogans into daily life; films and revolutionary operas dramatised model citizens. The 1963 ‘Learn from Comrade Lei Feng’ campaign turned a young soldier — said to have died selflessly serving the people — into the model of communist virtue. Children copied passages from his diary; classrooms held ‘Lei Feng study days’. Other ‘model citizens’ followed: the Dazhai brigade for agriculture, the Daqing oilfield workers for industry. Critics later argued that the Lei Feng diary was largely fabricated, but the campaign worked because it gave ordinary people a clear ideal to aspire to.

Mass rallies were the spectacle that pulled propaganda together. The eight Tiananmen rallies of August 1966 to November 1966 brought around 12 million Red Guards to Beijing, each clutching a Little Red Book and chanting ‘long live Chairman Mao’. For most participants this was the most exciting moment of their lives. Photographs of these rallies became propaganda in their own right, circulated to villages where peasants who would never travel to Beijing could see their leader surrounded by adoring youth.

The Cult of Mao

From 1964 onwards, the propaganda message narrowed onto Mao himself. Lin Biao, who replaced Peng Dehuai as Defence Minister in 1959, built the cult of Mao as a political weapon. He compiled the Little Red Book from Mao’s speeches, made it required reading inside the People’s Liberation Army, then expanded it nationwide. Soldiers held morning study sessions before duty; factory workers paused production for ‘asking instructions’ rituals before Mao’s portrait. Every public space displayed his image; statues went up in town squares.

A common student misconception is that the cult of Mao was endured cynically. Most Chinese, especially the young, genuinely believed. The cult worked because much of the propaganda was internalised — particularly during 1966–69, when Red Guards smashed temples and denounced teachers in the name of the Chairman they had been taught to revere from primary school. Strong answers acknowledge both the manufactured nature of the cult and the sincere belief it inspired.

Students often imagine that Chinese citizens went through propaganda rituals while privately rolling their eyes. Memoir evidence (Jung Chang’s Wild Swans, Mobo Gao’s village interviews, recent oral histories) shows that genuine veneration was widespread, especially among teenagers and young workers. Internalisation was the point: a loyal citizen polices themselves more cheaply than one watched by the police. Top-band answers distinguish between sincere belief in the early Cultural Revolution, ritual conformity by older intellectuals, and disillusionment among ‘sent-down’ youth after 1968.

Censorship

If propaganda was the loudspeaker, censorship was the muffler. The Ministry of Culture vetted every book, film, opera and newspaper. Foreign works deemed ‘bourgeois’ were banned; classical Chinese literature was attacked as feudal; private printing presses were closed. During the Cultural Revolution, Jiang Qing tightened the screws further, allowing only her ‘eight model operas’ on the public stage. Newspapers ran party-approved stories alone; the People’s Daily was the authoritative voice. Authors who fell out of favour — including the celebrated novelist Lao She, who drowned himself in 1966 after Red Guard struggle sessions — faced denunciation, beatings or worse.

Censorship worked alongside the propaganda machine: by removing alternative narratives, the regime made its own message the only one in circulation. Schools used party-written textbooks; libraries purged their shelves; family photographs of relatives in ‘bad class backgrounds’ were burned by their owners to avoid trouble. The 1957 Anti-Rightist Campaign, which had silenced the urban intelligentsia after the Hundred Flowers, made later censorship easier — the people most likely to resist had already been removed.

Laogai: Reform Through Labour

For those who could not be persuaded, there was the camp. The laogai system — literally ‘Reform Through Labour’ — was formalised in 1951. Hundreds of camps were built across China, particularly in the western provinces of Qinghai and Xinjiang. They held political prisoners (former GMD officials, denounced ‘rightists’, religious clergy, ‘capitalist roaders’) alongside ordinary criminals; the regime treated both as people whose thinking needed correcting through hard work. Inmates mined coal, farmed reclaimed land, built roads and produced manufactured goods. Estimates of the total detained vary widely; revisionist historians like Frank Dikötter put the figure in the millions during the Mao era.

A common misconception is that laogai was a wartime measure. It was not. It was a permanent Maoist institution, run continuously from 1951 to Mao’s death and beyond. The camps were also economic units, contributing to provincial production targets, which gave local cadres an incentive to keep them full. Inmates’ families were often informed only that a relative had been ‘sent away to study’.

Beyond camps and propaganda, surveillance ran through daily life. Every urban Chinese citizen belonged to a danwei (work unit) that controlled their job, housing, ration coupons and permission to marry. Neighbourhood committees, often headed by older women, watched comings and goings on every street. Each citizen had a dossier (dang’an) recording their class background, family history and political reliability — followed them through their career, decided promotions and informed denunciations. In the countryside, the production brigade played a similar role. Top-band students name these structures rather than describing ‘people watching each other’ in general.

Key Fact

Communist control rested on four pillars: propaganda (posters, loudspeakers, model citizens like Lei Feng), the cult of Mao (built by Lin Biao through the Little Red Book), censorship (Ministry of Culture, banned books, eight model operas) and forced labour (laogai, formalised in 1951). Surveillance through the danwei work unit and the personal dossier reached every citizen.

Historians Disagree

Western revisionist historians such as Frank Dikötter (The Cultural Revolution, 2016) and Roderick MacFarquhar treat the propaganda machine as an instrument of personal command, the laogai as systematic terror, and the cult of Mao as a deliberate political construction by Lin Biao and Jiang Qing’s Cultural Revolution Group. Sympathetic historians such as Mobo Gao (The Battle for China’s Past, 2008) argue the cult had genuine roots in popular feeling, that propaganda raised literacy and self-confidence in poor villages, and that the laogai numbers have been exaggerated in Cold War-era Western writing. Both views can be tested against the evidence; top-band answers acknowledge both rather than dismissing one as bias.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For interpretation questions on Communist control, examiners reward students who weigh top-down construction (Lin Biao’s Little Red Book, Jiang Qing’s eight operas, the laogai apparatus) against genuine internalisation (sincere belief by Red Guards, Lei Feng study sessions, danwei pressure). Use period-specific vocabulary — laogai, danwei, dossier, struggle session, Little Red Book, four olds — to lock in the SPaG marks on the 20-mark question. Avoid claiming ‘everyone secretly hated Mao’; cult belief was widespread, especially 1966–69, and strong answers say so explicitly.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Propaganda saturated public life through posters, loudspeakers, mass rallies and model citizens (Lei Feng, 1963), reaching village level despite low literacy.
  • The cult of Mao, built by Lin Biao via the Little Red Book (1964), peaked 1966–69 and was widely internalised, not endured cynically.
  • Censorship through the Ministry of Culture and Jiang Qing’s ‘eight model operas’, plus the laogai system (formalised 1951) and danwei surveillance, removed alternative voices and punished dissent.

lessons.title: Family Life, Women and the Marriage Law
lessons.description: Foot binding banned, communes splitting families and Mao’s claim that ‘women hold up half the sky’.
lessons.content_html:
A Society Built on Patriarchy

Before 1949 Chinese family life was shaped by Confucian patriarchy. Marriage was arranged by parents, often when the bride was a child; bride prices were paid; concubinage was legal in wealthy households; and female infanticide remained common in poor villages. Women’s feet had been bound from c.1100 onwards in elite families, breaking the bones of girls aged 4–7 to produce the prized ‘three-inch lotus’ foot — an excruciating practice that left women unable to walk far or work the fields. Although foot binding had been in long decline since the late Qing reforms of the 1900s and was banned by the Republican government in 1912, the practice persisted in remote villages into the 1940s.

Key Fact

The Marriage Law of 1 May 1950 made arranged marriage, bride price (the ‘sale’ of brides) and concubinage illegal. It established free choice in marriage, equal rights between husband and wife, and the right to divorce on either side — a revolutionary legal change that ran ahead of Chinese rural attitudes by decades.

The Marriage Law of 1950

The 1950 Marriage Law was one of the first major laws of the new People’s Republic. Drafted with input from Communist women activists such as Deng Yingchao (Zhou Enlai’s wife), it set the minimum marriage age at 20 for men and 18 for women, banned the buying and selling of brides, and gave both spouses equal rights in property and divorce. Women lined up at courthouses across China in 1950 and 1951 to file for divorce; in 1953 alone the courts handled around 1.1 million divorce cases. For young women trapped in childhood marriages, the law was liberation.

A common student misconception is that the Marriage Law was universally welcomed. In fact rural backlash was fierce. Husbands, mothers-in-law and clan elders saw the law as an attack on the family economy — a divorced wife could leave with property and remarry. Reports of beatings, suicides and murders of young women who tried to use the law’s provisions appeared in CCP investigations through the early 1950s. Some local cadres, themselves rural patriarchs, refused to enforce it. The 1953 enforcement campaign, ‘Marriage Law Implementation Month’, was launched precisely because the law was being widely ignored.

Top-band answers note that the law produced violent backlash, particularly in the countryside. CCP enforcement reports collected by historian Felix Wemheuer record beatings of young women, forced returns to abusive husbands and reports of suicides. The law was on paper revolutionary; in practice its impact was uneven, depending on whether local cadres enforced it. Use this to push back against any reading of Mao’s policies as smooth top-down emancipation.

Foot Binding Banned

Foot binding had been outlawed by the Republican government in 1912 but the practice continued in pockets of rural China through the 1940s. The CCP launched fresh campaigns in the early 1950s, sending women cadres into villages to inspect girls’ feet and prosecute parents who had bound them. By the late 1950s the practice was effectively extinct. Younger women regained the ability to walk normally and work in the fields and factories — a precondition of the workforce mobilisation that followed.

Communes Disrupt the Family

If the Marriage Law reshaped marriage, the communes of 1958 reshaped the family itself. Around 26,000 people’s communes absorbed roughly 99% of rural households. Family cooking was banned in favour of communal mess halls (about 3.4 million across China by mid-1959); childcare was collective; private plots were abolished. The CCP slogan was ‘production over kinship’. Women were enlisted en masse into the workforce, while older women ran nurseries and kitchens. For working women, this meant relief from the ‘double burden’ of paid labour plus domestic chores — in theory.

In practice the communes’ disruption of family life was deeply unpopular. The mess halls were poorly run, food was wasted, and during the 1959–62 famine they became sites of starvation. After the famine, Liu Shaoqi’s recovery measures (1962–65) quietly returned cooking to the household and re-allowed small private plots. The commune as an organisation survived until 1983, but the radical attack on the household economy did not last.

Women in the Workforce

Mao’s most quoted line on women is ‘women hold up half the sky’. Female labour-force participation rose dramatically: by 1976 around 90% of urban women of working age had paid work, an extraordinary figure by world standards. Propaganda celebrated iron girls — teenage girls in tractor brigades, oil-field work crews and steel mills, photographed driving heavy machinery and lifting sacks of grain. Jiang Qing, Mao’s fourth wife and the only woman in the senior leadership, became a powerful figure during the Cultural Revolution.

A second misconception is that Mao gave women equality. The reality was more limited. Women’s pay was lower (commonly counted as 7 work points to a man’s 10); housework was unchanged, leaving women with the ‘double burden’; the Politburo remained almost entirely male. Soong Ching-ling (widow of Sun Yat-sen) and Deng Yingchao were senior figures, but Jiang Qing’s power came from her marriage to Mao, not promotion through the party. After the Gang of Four was arrested in 1976, the iron-girl propaganda was quietly retired and gender norms in the countryside reasserted themselves.

Western revisionist historians like Frank Dikötter (The Tragedy of Liberation) emphasise the violence of the Marriage Law’s rural enforcement and the gulf between Mao’s rhetoric and women’s pay packets. Sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao argue that the Mao era genuinely transformed women’s lives — literacy, paid work, the end of foot binding, the right to divorce — in ways the post-1978 reform era did not match. Both can be tested against the evidence. Strong answers note specific gains (legal divorce, end of foot binding, mass literacy, near-universal urban employment) and specific limits (rural backlash, pay gap, double burden, almost no women in the senior leadership).

Key Fact

Genuine gains: end of foot binding, legal right to divorce (1950), mass literacy, near-universal urban employment by 1976. Limits: rural backlash against the Marriage Law, lower female pay (often 7 work points to a man’s 10), unchanged housework, almost no women in the Politburo. Mao’s slogan was ‘women hold up half the sky’; the reality was uneven.

Use period-specific vocabulary — Marriage Law, work points, iron girls, double burden, foot binding — to lock in SPaG marks. Avoid claims that Mao ‘liberated’ or ‘failed’ women in absolute terms; the picture is mixed and the highest band rewards balance.

Key Takeaways

  • The 1950 Marriage Law banned arranged marriage, bride price and concubinage; gave women the right to divorce; sparked rural backlash and 1.1 million divorce cases by 1953.
  • Foot binding, in long decline since 1912, was effectively ended by 1950s campaigns — releasing women into the workforce.
  • The 1958 communes disrupted family life through mess halls and collective childcare, then quietly retreated after the 1959–62 famine; women’s gains in education and employment were real but came with the ‘double burden’ and a continuing pay gap.

lessons.title: Education, Health and Cultural Change
lessons.description: Barefoot doctors, simplified characters and smashed temples — life rebuilt from above.
lessons.content_html:
A Country to be Re-educated

In 1949 around 80% of Chinese adults could not read. Most villages had no clinic; trained doctors clustered in the cities; life expectancy was c.36 years. Buddhism, Daoism, Christianity, Islam and ancestor worship shaped daily ritual. Mao’s regime set out to rebuild all three pillars of everyday life — education, health and culture — from above. The means were the propaganda machine, the work-unit (danwei) supervision system and, after 1966, the violence of the Red Guards. The results were genuinely transformative in some areas (literacy, rural healthcare) and devastating in others (the closure of universities, the destruction of religious sites).

Key Fact

Adult literacy rose from around 20% in 1949 to around 70% by 1976. Pinyin was introduced in 1958, alongside simplified characters — both designed to accelerate mass literacy among peasants and workers.

Education before 1966

From 1949 the CCP launched literacy campaigns aimed at adults: village classes ran in winter when farm work was light, and worker classes ran in factories. The 1958 introduction of simplified characters reduced the strokes needed to write thousands of common words; Pinyin gave a Roman-letter system for teaching pronunciation and indexing dictionaries. Together they cut the time needed to reach functional literacy. Soviet aid helped build new universities and technical institutes during the First Five-Year Plan; gaokao, the national university entrance examination, ran competitively until 1966.

Education was framed as service to the revolution. Schoolchildren learned arithmetic alongside passages of Mao’s thought; agricultural and industrial work experience was built into the curriculum from primary school. By 1965, primary enrolment had reached around 80% of children of school age — a sharp gain on the pre-1949 figure of c.20%. Women’s and girls’ literacy rose particularly rapidly because the campaigns explicitly targeted them.

The Collapse of Education after 1966

The Cultural Revolution wrecked formal education. From May 1966, schools and universities across China closed. The gaokao was abolished and would not return until 1977. Teachers were denounced as ‘stinking ninth’ (the bottom of a hierarchy of class enemies); some were beaten to death by their own pupils. Universities reopened from 1970 with admission by class background and political reliability rather than examination, and the curriculum was reduced to revolutionary slogans plus practical work. From 1968 onwards, around 17 million urban ‘sent-down youth’ were dispatched to the countryside under the xiaxiang campaign, in theory to learn from peasants, in practice to disperse the Red Guards Mao no longer needed.

A common student misconception is that all education collapsed. Primary literacy classes in villages mostly continued, run by local cadres rather than universities; barefoot doctors’ basic training expanded; and propaganda materials reached far more peasants than Republican-era schoolbooks ever had. The collapse was concentrated at secondary and higher education, where a generation lost ten years of formal study. Strong answers separate the gains for primary literacy from the catastrophe for higher education.

The barefoot doctor system was a real success — rural infant mortality fell sharply, life expectancy rose from c.36 in 1949 to c.66 by 1976, and basic vaccination reached parts of the countryside that had never seen a clinic. But healthcare was uneven: most trained doctors had been forced from cities to villages against their will after 1965, hospitals remained concentrated in urban centres, and the regime suppressed reporting of the 1959–62 famine death rates. Top-band answers note both: a genuine transformation of rural healthcare and the political suppression of evidence about its costs.

Healthcare and the Barefoot Doctors

Pre-1949 China had perhaps 40,000 trained doctors for c.500 million people, mostly clustered in coastal cities. Mao attacked this as bourgeois medicine. The barefoot doctors programme, formalised in 1965, trained around one million paramedical workers in three to six months and dispatched them to communes. They carried a basic kit of medicines, taught hygiene, delivered vaccinations and ran family-planning clinics. By 1976 most communes had at least one barefoot doctor; rural infant mortality fell sharply; and life expectancy rose from c.36 in 1949 to c.66 by 1976.

Healthcare was not uniformly transformed. Trained doctors sent down to villages from 1965 often resented the move; cities lost specialist services; the worst famine years were not addressed by additional medical capacity but by the suppression of death reporting. Zhou Enlai privately pushed back against some of the most disruptive Cultural Revolution attacks on hospitals, but he could not prevent the chaos in major cities. Even so, by Western metrics the Mao era’s rural healthcare gains are widely acknowledged, including by sympathetic historians like Mobo Gao.

Attacks on Traditional Culture

From May 1966 the regime declared war on the ‘four olds’ — old customs, old culture, old habits, old ideas. Red Guards smashed Buddhist temples, Daoist shrines and Christian churches; Confucius’s tomb at Qufu was desecrated by Red Guards in November 1966 in a deliberate act of symbolic destruction. Mosques in the Hui Muslim regions and Tibetan Buddhist monasteries were attacked particularly violently. After the 1959 Tibetan uprising and the Dalai Lama’s flight to India, monasteries had already been closed in large numbers; the Cultural Revolution finished the job, with most of Tibet’s c.6,000 monasteries reportedly destroyed or damaged. Christianity, Islam and Buddhism were treated as foreign or feudal; clergy were paraded in struggle sessions, beaten and imprisoned; family ancestor altars were burned by their own owners under pressure from neighbourhood committees.

A misconception is that all religion was permanently extinguished. Folk and ancestor practices survived underground — in many villages the smashed altar was rebuilt as soon as the Red Guards left. After Mao’s death in 1976, enforcement relaxed; Deng Xiaoping’s reforms allowed limited reopening of temples and churches under state supervision. But the cultural damage of 1966–76 was irreversible: many ancient buildings, manuscripts, statues and artworks were destroyed.

As the wife of Mao and a former Shanghai actress, Jiang Qing took charge of culture during the Cultural Revolution. She banned almost all classical Chinese opera, foreign films and traditional novels, replacing them with eight ‘model operas’ (yangbanxi) such as Taking Tiger Mountain by Strategy and The Red Detachment of Women. These operas were performed by state troupes, broadcast on radio, filmed and shown in every cinema; for nearly a decade they were almost the only live theatre or cinema available. Top-band answers name them as a deliberate cultural project, not just a destructive impulse: Jiang Qing was building a new revolutionary culture to replace what was being smashed.

Key Fact

Genuine reforms: literacy from c.20% to c.70%, Pinyin (1958) and simplified characters, c.1 million barefoot doctors (1965+), life expectancy from c.36 to c.66. Major losses: schools and universities closed 1966–77 with gaokao abolished; Confucius’s tomb desecrated 1966; most of Tibet’s c.6,000 monasteries destroyed or damaged; almost all classical opera replaced by Jiang Qing’s eight model operas.

Use period-specific vocabulary — Pinyin, gaokao, xiaxiang, barefoot doctors, four olds, model operas, danwei — to lock in SPaG marks. Avoid framing this as either a uniform success or a uniform disaster; the highest band rewards the both/and judgement, supported by named figures and dates.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Education: literacy rose from c.20% (1949) to c.70% (1976) using Pinyin and simplified characters, but the Cultural Revolution closed schools and universities and abolished the gaokao from 1966 to 1977.
  • Health: the c.1 million barefoot doctors (formalised 1965) raised rural healthcare and lifted life expectancy from c.36 to c.66, though urban specialist care declined and famine death rates were suppressed.
  • Culture: the ‘four olds’ campaign smashed temples, churches and monasteries (Confucius’s tomb 1966; Tibet from 1959); Jiang Qing’s eight model operas replaced almost all classical theatre and film for nearly a decade.
